title: Proposal 2: Prohibit Campaign Contributions From Certain Regulated Utilities and Government Contractors

context.text: Citizen-initiated statute proposed by the committee Michiganders for Money Out of Politics. The Board of State Canvassers certified the petition 3-1 on July 24, 2026, finding the campaign cleared the 356,958-signature threshold by a single-digit margin in the sampled review (the committee had submitted 561,282 signatures). Because the Legislature did not adopt it, it goes to the November ballot; the Board approved the ballot language on August 17, 2026. An opposition committee, Protect MI Free Speech, challenged the signatures, and the measure survived a Michigan Supreme Court challenge before the ballot was finalized.

question.text: A PROPOSED INITIATED LAW TO PROHIBIT CAMPAIGN CONTRIBUTIONS FROM CERTAIN REGULATED UTILITIES AND GOVERNMENT CONTRACTORS AND APPLY CAMPAIGN FINANCE LAWS AND REGULATIONS TO ADDITIONAL TYPES OF POLITICAL COMMUNICATIONS. The proposal would prohibit regulated electric and gas utilities, contractors with over $250,000 annually in government contracts, and people and organizations with substantial connections to these utilities/contractors from making direct or indirect campaign contributions to those who run for or hold offices that impact them. Expand laws regulating spending on political communications, including those requiring disclosing donor information, to apply to communications clearly identifying candidates or ballot questions, even if they do not expressly advocate voting for/against them. Expressly apply the law requiring disclosure of who paid for political communications to internet political communications. Should this proposal be adopted?

summary.text: According to the Citizens Research Council of Michigan (as reported by Michigan Advance), the initiative amends the Michigan Campaign Finance Act to require "paid for by" disclosures on certain internet political ads, expand donor and spending disclosure for certain political ads, and restrict contributions from rate-regulated gas and electric utilities and state and local contractors with more than $250,000 in annual contracts. The restrictions also cover owners with a 5% or greater stake, board members, executives and their family members, and lobbyists. There would be an 18-month implementation period for the contractor ban; a knowing violation could lead to contract cancellation and a one-year contracting ban. Once enacted, amending it would take a three-fourths vote of the House and Senate. The Council noted likely free-speech challenges and possible enforcement costs; the Senate Fiscal Agency's fiscal estimate is under fiscal impact.

measure.yesMeans: Enacts the initiated law: regulated electric and gas utilities, government contractors with over $250,000 in annual contracts, and people and organizations with substantial connections to them could not make direct or indirect contributions to those who run for or hold offices that affect them, and political-communication disclosure rules would be expanded, including to internet communications.
measure.noMeans: Leaves current law in place, which does not limit contributions from regulated utilities and large government contractors in this way.

argumentsFor.text: Christy McGillivray, co-chair of Michiganders for Money Out of Politics: "Michiganders are ready to finally rein in pay-to-play politics and out-of-control political spending in Lansing this November."

Michael Brady, attorney for Michiganders for Money Out of Politics: "What we have here today is the culmination of thousands of Michiganders, Michigan citizens, Republicans, Democrats and independents, exercising their constitutional and statutory right to reform their government."

argumentsAgainst.text: Michigan Chamber of Commerce statement (issued when the proposed language was posted; the Chamber is not identified in the sources as the registered opposition committee): the proposal "appears to silence the voices of job providers and limit free speech for some while giving others, like labor unions, a free pass."

John Sellek, spokesperson for the opposition committee Protect MI Free Speech: "The gist of what we have to do between now and November 3 is to educate people that nothing is as simple as it appears on the surface. They need to understand all the pros and cons before they vote on this in the fall."

currentLaw.text: Per the Senate Fiscal Agency, the Michigan Campaign Finance Act already regulates contributions and spending and requires disclosure of who pays for specified advertisements, and companies and individuals are subject to the same standards. Thirty-eight states require sponsor disclosure on internet communications; Michigan does not. Currently any person may give an unlimited amount to PACs running electioneering communications without the donor being reported; the PAC's name, but not its contributors, must be disclosed. The proposal would add the utility and contractor contribution prohibitions and expand the Act's definitions and disclosure rules.

fiscalImpact.text: Senate Fiscal Agency: a minor negative fiscal impact on the Department of the Attorney General (costs of suing utilities that refuse to pay fines; a high volume of cases could require one or more additional full-time positions, about $145,700 each per year); a minor negative impact on State district courts from new misdemeanor cases; negative and corresponding positive impacts on local government (jail and court costs, offset by fines up to $1,000 and civil fines on utilities of up to 10 times the contribution, which fund local libraries; amount indeterminate); and a possible negative impact on the Department of State, which could need one or more additional full-time positions depending on the number of investigations.

supporters.text: Michiganders for Money Out of Politics (sponsoring ballot question committee; co-chair Christy McGillivray)

opponents.text: Protect MI Free Speech (registered ballot question committee opposing the proposal; spokesperson John Sellek)
Michigan Chamber of Commerce (statement opposing the proposal; the committee's treasurer, Wendy Block, is described by Bridge Michigan as the Chamber's head lobbyist)
Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan and CMS Energy (Consumers Energy's parent) (contributors to Protect MI Free Speech who said the proposal would silence their employees)

campaignFinance.text: Opposing: Protect MI Free Speech had received a total of $579,000 in contributions as of a July 27, 2026 campaign finance disclosure, per Michigan Advance, including $50,000 from the DTE-affiliated group Michigan Energy First and cumulative $65,000 each from CMS Energy Corporation and Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan. A total for Michiganders for Money Out of Politics was not found in the sources reviewed, and no later filing totals were located.

researchNotes: Michigan publishes no state voter pamphlet with official arguments. The ballot language is the Board of State Canvassers' August 17, 2026 text as reproduced by Michigan Advance and WCMU's ballot guide (a Board draft in the August 17 agenda lacked 'AND GOVERNMENT CONTRACTORS' in the title; the approved version has it). Signature counts are from the Bureau of Elections staff report. Sellek's statement for the registered opposition committee (Protect MI Free Speech) is a general statement rather than a substantive argument; its attorney's signature-gathering criticism is a process objection and is not used. The Citizens Research Council's observations about free-speech challenges appear in the summary rather than as an argument. The Michigan Chamber of Commerce is not identified in the sources as the registered opposition committee. Fiscal and current-law sections are from the Senate Fiscal Agency overview. The $579,000 opposition total is the July 27 disclosure as reported by Michigan Advance; supporters' totals and later filings were not found. No fullTextUrl: the petition text was not located in the sources reviewed.
